title: Rethinking AR Productivity Metrics in 2023: New Insights
summary: Explore how AR productivity metrics go beyond activity counts, focusing on cash collection, denial resolution, and meaningful account advancement.
body_markdown:
*By Vanessa C*


**Summary:** In 2023, effective AR productivity metrics focus on understanding the underlying causes of AR changes rather than just activity metrics. Key insights include analyzing where AR is concentrated, scrutinizing write-offs, and differentiating between accounting maneuvers and actual collections. True productivity involves meaningful interactions and proper documentation, while balancing volume and quality is essential for effective AR management.


The Monday morning dashboard can show a significant number of accounts closed for each collector, while cash receipts decreased in that same pay period. In patient financial services, counting touches gives department heads a neat-looking sense of speed, and unresolved balances keep drifting past the 90-day mark. According to[TechTarget RevCycleIntelligence](https://www.techtarget.com/revcyclemanagement/news/366625109/Initial-claim-denial-rates-put-revenue-cycle-in-tough-spot) , hospital networks had an initial claim denial rate of 11.81% in 2024. If leaders chase that volume with generic touch counts, they reward people for opening a chart, typing a bland note, and setting a follow-up date thirty days away.


To find the AR productivity metrics that actually matter, you have to separate physical account handling from real financial resolution. Revenue cycle directors who look at aging spreads, write-off causes, and touch-to-cash ratios start to see why busy teams can still leave millions sitting there.


## Why AR Reduction Isn't Always a Win


Gross accounts receivable balances can fall fast while collections stay flat. When leadership cheers a drop in gross AR and skips the general ledger offsets, they mix up balance sheet write-downs with actual collection work. Real recovery means liquid cash deposits from commercial and government payers. A lower total AR balance often hides aggressive back-office cleanups, unapplied cash errors, or bad debt dumps started to hit artificial quarter targets.


### The Impact of Write-Offs


Contractual adjustments and uncollectible write-offs clear workqueues without putting dollars into the operating account. When hospital teams write off aged balances under small-balance thresholds or timely filing expirations, they make the aging buckets look cleaner than they are.


Audit the write-off reason codes against specific collector IDs, and you can tell whether accounts were truly uncollectible or simply left alone after two unanswered status checks. Track net collections as a share of gross charges, and staff lose the easy hiding place behind administrative adjustments.


### Transfers and Adjustments


Moving aged self-pay balances to early-out vendors or secondary bad debt agencies clears hospital ledgers on paper. Those transfers create the look of fast resolution while collection fees eat into the net recovery. Supervisors need to watch credit balances, internal clearing accounts, and payer-to-payer adjustments as separate lines. Monthly ledger audits keep staff from shuffling stalled claims across workqueues just to reset the account touch timer.


## Concentration of AR: A Key Insight


Average days in AR can hide ugly liquidity pockets inside certain payer contracts or clinical departments. A facility sitting at a steady 42 days in AR might still carry a nasty spike in aged cardiology claims or one commercial payer holding remittances back. Concentration metrics show where capital stays trapped before accounts hit filing limits. Split active inventory by payer, clinical specialty, and CARC denial code, and senior follow-up staff can focus on the claims that are choking cash flow.


### Aging Buckets and Payer Patterns


Put accounts receivable into 30, 60, 90, and 120-day buckets, and the payer stalls start to stand out. If a regional commercial payer contributes to gross revenue but holds a large portion of claims aged past 90 days, the problem may lie with payer behavior or the contract's adjudication rules. Compare each payer's average turnaround with the contracted clean-claim payment window, and revenue cycle leaders have the leverage they need for joint operating committee meetings. Claims that linger beyond 60 days call for root-cause review before secondary appeals lapse.


### Service Line Analysis


Surgical suites, infusion centers, and emergency departments all bring different documentation, pre-authorization, and billing rules. When orthopedic claims produce high initial denials, the bottleneck usually starts with implant invoice attachments or operative notes, not routine billing lag.


Break aging metrics out by clinical service line, and operational leaders can see whether denials begin in clinical documentation, mid-revenue cycle coding, or patient access registration. That kind of separation lets managers fix the structural break instead of telling follow-up collectors to call payers again and again.


## Activity vs. Progress: The Real Measure


A collector who works eighty claims a day by reviewing clearinghouse edits and resetting follow-up dates can still produce zero cash yield. Counting account touches without checking what happened next rewards speed over adjudication.


Operational productivity has to measure actions that move a balance toward final remittance or a formal appeal. If an interaction does not correct billing data, supply the requested medical records, or secure a firm check disbursement date, the account was touched rather than resolved.


### Meaningful Interactions


A meaningful payer interaction leaves behind a concrete transaction reference number, an itemized denial explanation, or a promise to reprocess the claim. A routine portal check that only says a claim is pending, while skipping the missing attachment, burns staff time for nothing. Follow-up staff need to verify the line-level adjudication, confirm the medical necessity review, and write down the formal tracking number on each call. When collectors log the actual adjudication steps, passive follow-up turns into directed collections.


### Documentation of Progress


If notes are vague, the next billing specialist starts over and spends twenty minutes digging through old account activity. Standard note templates push collectors to record the representative's name, the call reference number, the exact denial reason, and the action taken.


Structured notes give supervisors a way to see whether the collector actually cleared the billing barrier. Clear documentation also creates direct accountability across shifts, and it cuts down on duplicate calls for claims that are still open.


## Balancing Productivity and Quality


Pushing for high daily account volume without checking collection quality produces shallow work and bigger write-offs. Staff who have to hit eighty accounts a day will skip complex appeals and take the easy claim-status checks. A workable operational standard weighs account volume against appeal success rates, overturn percentages, and cash collected per hour. If the team is touching a lot of accounts but bringing in little cash, they are cycling through queues instead of resolving them.


### Quality Reviews


Quality assurance audits have to sample closed accounts at random and check whether collectors followed standard operating procedures. Auditors look at whether staff fixed clearinghouse rejections, appealed clinical denials within contract limits, and attached the required documentation. Scoring accounts for analytical thoroughness and compliance helps revenue cycle managers find collectors who drop collectable revenue just to hit quota targets. Regular scoring also points out training gaps across the department before payer filing limits run out.


### Training and Development


Payer policy manuals and billing requirements change constantly across commercial health plans, Medicare Advantage, and Medicaid managed care. Giving collectors deep training on CARC and RARC codes, coordination of benefits rules, and medical necessity appeals speeds up claim recovery.


Regular operational workshops build internal knowledge around complex claims. Skilled collectors spot payer adjudication errors faster, which cuts the average number of touches needed to settle disputed balances.


## Tailoring Productivity Expectations


One-size-fits-all volume quotas fail because a basic eligibility rejection takes far less effort than building a clinical denial appeal. If every desk is expected to handle sixty touches a day, workers on complex specialty queues will cut corners or drop difficult balances.


Productivity benchmarks have to reflect the cognitive work and administrative steps each queue demands. A specialist building level-two ERISA appeals might reasonably handle fifteen high-dollar accounts a day, while an electronic clearinghouse edit queue calls for eighty.


That segmented quota model falls apart during an unexpected clearinghouse outage or a major payer portal shutdown, such as the 2024 Change Healthcare disruption. Once the electronic links break completely, normal complexity tiers stop mattering, and patient financial services teams have to move every available staff member into emergency batch re-submissions, manual paper filings, and mixed work queues to protect basic cash reserves.


### Differentiating Account Types


Splitting AR inventories by difficulty level gives each billing desk fairer benchmarks. Routine clearinghouse rejection edits need fast, high-volume handling, while high-dollar trauma or oncology appeals call for detailed clinical chart reviews. Separating simple demographic fixes from complex medical necessity disputes helps keep staff from burning out. Different touch quotas for each workqueue type let management hold people to standards that fit the role.


### Adjusting Workflows


Reworking patient financial services into specialized resolution units keeps complex balances from getting stuck behind high-volume tasks. Routine claims move through automated rule sweeps and junior status checkers, while experienced reimbursement specialists handle the harder payer disputes.


Matching employee skill levels with specific denial types improves cash recovery speed. This split also keeps technical denials from aging past appeal windows while junior billers clear demographic edits.


## Leadership's Role in Prioritization


Without clear direction from management, billing teams tend to chase low-balance, easy claims because those help daily volume targets. If prioritization stays with each person's judgment, seven-figure balances sit in aging queues while filing windows close. Revenue cycle leaders need objective workqueue rules built around expected reimbursement value, aging thresholds, and payer filing rules. Those rules tell collectors which balances should go first each morning.


### Setting Clear Guidelines


Automated workqueue sorting rules should put high-dollar, high-risk accounts at the top of the daily collector list.


The logic needs to weigh timely filing deadlines, remaining appeal limits, and open balances when it builds the day's order. Clear operating rules cut out guesswork from the collector's daily routine. When billers work from queues that have already been sorted by priority, revenue teams protect major hospital dollars from expiring.


### Communicating Priorities


Payer backlogs and sudden policy changes force supervisors to shift team focus without delay. Morning huddles and weekly department updates keep frontline staff aware of new clearinghouse delays or targeted payer projects.


Direct communication spells out when teams need to move from routine aging queues to specific denial cleanup projects. Strong managerial direction keeps the department aimed at primary cash collection goals.


## Regular Checkpoints for Continuous Improvement


Bi-weekly operational checkpoints stop stale balances from sitting through quarterly reporting cycles. These sessions review stuck accounts, repeated payer delays, and high-balance inventory that needs immediate executive attention. An operational checkpoint exists to define next steps, not to repeat static balance sheet figures. Looking at specific stuck accounts exposes internal process flaws that call for fast cross-department fixes.


### Structured Meetings


Meetings stay useful when leadership sticks to a defined agenda instead of drifting into vague admin talk. Sessions should focus on specific aged claims, unresolved high-dollar disputes, and repeat denial reasons across major payers. Managers should leave each operational checkpoint with named account owners, concrete action items, and firm due dates. Tight meeting discipline keeps hard payer rejections in front of executives until they are resolved.


### Feedback Loops


Direct communication between billing collectors and patient access managers stops repeated billing mistakes at the front door. When follow-up teams spot recurring demographic or pre-authorization rejections, patient registration teams can change intake steps right away.


Reliable data loops across departments keep administrative errors from reaching final billing. Front-end fixes cut later claim rejections and speed clean claim payment rates.


## Group Learning Through Shared Checkpoints


Organizing operational checkpoints around shared payer contracts or clinical lines builds collective expertise across the billing office. Collectors who work the same commercial payer run into the same adjudication problems and portal errors.


Reviewing complex claims together turns isolated escalations into standard practice for the whole department. Team reviews keep individual collectors from repeating the same research on shared payer patterns.


### Collaborative Problem-Solving


Looking at difficult account rejections in team settings surfaces recovery methods that individual staff members found on their own. A specialist who found an unlisted payer fax line or a better appeal argument can pass that route to peers.


Collaborative analysis brings practical answers to stubborn payer delays. Spreading those day-to-day workarounds across the revenue cycle department speeds recovery on stalled balances.


### Consistent Guidance


Group reviews keep all billing specialists using the same appeal strategies and write-off protocols across client portfolios. Standardizing follow-up practices cuts down erratic billing decisions and irregular adjustment approvals across the department.


Consistent guidance leads to uniform work across all active workqueues. Standard operating habits protect clean claim rates and keep team documentation matched to internal audit standards.


## Importance of Documentation Standards


Vague account notes like "called payer, pending review" hide unproductive work and force duplicate investigations on later touches. Standardized documentation standards call for clear records of what the specialist checked, what data was sent, and when the payer needs to respond.


Strong documentation protects hospital collections during payer audits and makes handoffs smoother when collectors move between queues. Clear notes speed quality checks and show exactly where an account stalled.


### Standardizing Documentation


Standardized note formats require billers to record the specific contact channel, representative identification, reference number, and detailed denial breakdown. Mandating standardized notes removes ambiguity regarding what took place during the touch.


Consistent documentation structures make operational audits straightforward and objective. Supervisors can quickly determine whether the collector performed appropriate follow-up or merely logged an empty touch to inflate daily counts.


### Leveraging Technology


Deploying automated note templates and direct system integrations relieves billing specialists of repetitive manual data entry. Pre-populated macros record routine portal status checks and clearinghouse updates directly into the hospital electronic health record.


Automating administrative documentation allows collectors to spend their hours analyzing complex claim rejections and filing appeals. Modern operational tools maintain complete audit trails while cutting follow-up handling time.


## Beyond Cash: Comprehensive AR Performance


Cash collection remains the primary goal of patient financial services, but evaluating staff exclusively on collected dollars overlooks critical preventative value. Billing teams protect hospital solvency by overturning improper denials, eliminating aging backlogs, and discovering payer adjudication defects.


Evaluating staff across multiple operational dimensions produces a resilient revenue cycle organization. Teams that identify billing issues early prevent future cash interruptions and protect net operating margins.


### Trend Identification


Analyzing denial patterns across clinical specialties and payer IDs uncovers systemic billing discrepancies before they compound into major losses. If a commercial payer abruptly begins rejecting a specific evaluation code, billing staff can notify health system compliance and coding teams immediately.


Tracking denial frequency trends provides the operational insight needed to adjust billing scrubbers and claim rules. Early trend detection protects hospital cash flow from widespread payer policy shifts.


### Preventing Recurring Issues


Correcting the root causes of recurring billing rejections stops future claim delays permanently. When billing specialists partner with clinical departments to correct charge master discrepancies or order sets, clean claim pass rates rise.


Stopping administrative errors at their clinical source permanently cuts downstream AR collection costs. Preventing claim denials protects health system cash reserves far more effectively than hiring additional staff to rework broken claims.


## LunaBill: A Partner in AR Management


Modern revenue cycle leaders deploy artificial intelligence to remove routine manual follow-up from billing queues entirely.[LunaBill](https://lunabill.com/) deploys a coordinated team of 13 specialized AI agents that works accounts receivable queues directly inside systems like Epic, Cerner, and GoRev without adding internal headcount. The system automates routine payer portal inquiries, places live payer telephone calls, deciphers CARC and RARC denial codes, submits appeals, and posts detailed reference notes back to the primary billing system.


At Nutex Health, a 24-campus health system operating on Epic and GoRev, LunaBill processed more than $32M of accounts receivable in 30 days with zero added staff. Across commercial claims aged past 60 days, days in AR dropped from 45 to 7 within three months of deployment. By delegating high-volume payer follow-up to automated systems, health systems free senior reimbursement specialists to focus on high-dollar clinical disputes and complex escalations.


## Conclusion


Audit the last one hundred accounts marked as resolved in your primary aging queue. Separate those balances into true cash collections, contractual write-offs, and administrative adjustments to uncover your real touch-to-cash conversion rate. Calculate the average touches required to resolve commercial claims aged past 60 days, then compare that figure against your write-off percentages.


Next, reconfigure daily workqueues to prioritize high-dollar accounts and short timely filing deadlines ahead of volume quotas. Replace generic daily touch counts with metrics that measure appeal overturn rates, root-cause denial documentation, and aging movement. Building an effective accounts receivable operation takes strict queue segmentation, standardized documentation rules, and automated follow-up tools that convert open claims into collected cash.
